It first queries the variable’s definition; if defined, it returns the value of that definition. If not defined, it falls back to whether global debug or trace flags are set.

@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::PolicyPushP.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::PolicyPushP.body: Stores a reference to the supplied `cmMakefile` instance and immediately invokes its `PushPolicy()` method, thereby applying the current policy context for the duration of the object’s lifetime.

@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::PolicyPushP.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::PolicyPushP.body:
The `PolicyPushPop` helper embodies a RAII guard that temporarily installs a policy value on a global stack and guarantees its automatic removal when the guard goes out of scope. The class is deliberately non‑copyable (`PolicyPushPop(const PolicyPushPop&) = delete;`) to prevent accidental duplication of the temporary policy state, which would otherwise break the invariant that the policy is popped exactly once. The typical usage pattern is:

```cpp
{
    PolicyPushPop guard(policy);   // pushes the policy
    … // code that runs under the policy
}   // guard’s destructor automatically pops the policy
```

@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::operator=@k.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::operator=@k.body: The deleted assignment operator stops any attempt to copy or re‑assign an existing `PolicyPushPop` object; the compiler will generate an error if you try to use `=` on an instance, ensuring its state remains unchanged after construction.

@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::~PolicyPush.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PolicyPushPop::~PolicyPush.body: When an instance of `PolicyPushPop` goes out of scope, its destructor automatically calls `PopPolicy()` on its internal `Makefile`, effectively reverting the last policy that was pushed onto the policy stack.

@lcmMakefile::PopFunctionBlockerBarrier@.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopFunctionBlockerBarrier@.body: When invoked, the routine pops all function‑blocker objects that were added after the last barrier marker. It removes each top‑of‑stack object until the stored “barrier” index is reached, optionally emitting a fatal error message for any block that was opened but never closed. After the cleanup, the barrier marker itself is discarded.

@lcmMakefile::PopFunctionScope@k_ZN10cmM.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopFunctionScope@k_ZN10cmM.body: The function collapses the current function‑level context: it first clears any policy‑state, then restores the snapshot and releases the function‑blocker barrier. If the build is not in boot‑strap mode it also releases the global file‑lock pool entry, and finally pops any loop‑block barrier that was active.

@lcmMakefile::PopLoopBlock@k_ZN10cmMakef.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopLoopBlock@k_ZN10cmMakef.body: This method decrements the top counter on `LoopBlockCounter`. It verifies the stack is non‑empty and that the current counter is positive before decrementing, effectively popping the current loop‑block depth.

@lcmMakefile::PopLoopBlockBarrier@k_ZN10.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopLoopBlockBarrier@k_ZN10.body: The function removes the current loop‑block counter entry after a loop has finished. It first verifies that the stack isn’t empty (an invariant that must hold), then checks that the top of the counter stack is zero (meaning the outermost loop block’s reference count has dropped to zero). Finally it pops that entry from the stack to clean up the state.

@lcmMakefile::PopMacroScope@k_ZN10cmMake.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopMacroScope@k_ZN10cmMake.body: The function removes the current macro scope by performing three ordered clean‑ups: it first invokes the policy‑level pop, then clears the snapshot (optionally reporting an error), and finally lifts the function‑blocker barrier. Each step finalizes a different part of the macro’s lifecycle, ensuring the remaining state is stable for subsequent parsing.

@lcmMakefile::PopPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefile.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefile.body: Verifies that a pop is only issued when a corresponding push has been performed, otherwise it logs a fatal error.

@lcmMakefile::PopScope@k_ZN10cmMakefile8.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopScope@k_ZN10cmMakefile8.body: On invocation, `PopScope` cleans up the current function scope: it first (when not in bootstrap mode) tells the global file‑lock pool to discard the top‑level function scope, then removes any pending loop‑block barriers and finally restores the previous snapshot state.

@lcmMakefile::PopSnapshot@k_ZN10cmMakefi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PopSnapshot@k_ZN10cmMakefi.body: The routine iteratively disposes any open policy scopes that belong to the current snapshot, optionally signalling a fatal error when an unmatched `PUSH` is detected, and finally restores the snapshot to the one that was active before the current snapshot was created—confirming that the new snapshot remains valid.

@lcmMakefile::PrintCommandTrace@k_ZNK10c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PrintCommandTrace@k_ZNK10c.body: PrintCommandTrace records a command execution event. It first verifies whether the current file is in the trace list, expands any variables in the arguments, then formats the command and its arguments either in JSON or human‑readable form and writes the entry to a trace file or, if none is set, to standard output.

@lcmMakefile::PushFunctionBlockerBarrier.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PushFunctionBlockerBarrier.body: The routine records the current index of the function blocker list by appending the size of `FunctionBlockers` to `FunctionBlockerBarriers`.

@lcmMakefile::PushFunctionScope@k_ZN10cm.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PushFunctionScope@k_ZN10cm.body: It saves the current compiler state, opens a new function‑level scope, locks the file (unless bootstrapping), and then applies the supplied policy map.

@lcmMakefile::PushLoopBlock@k_ZN10cmMake.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PushLoopBlock@k_ZN10cmMake.body: Increment the counter that tracks the current depth of a nested loop block. The method assumes the stack already contains an entry, so it simply bumps the top‑value up by one.

@lcmMakefile::PushLoopBlockBarrier@k_ZN1.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PushLoopBlockBarrier@k_ZN1.body: Pushes a zero onto the LoopBlockCounter stack to record the start of a new loop block.

@lcmMakefile::PushMacroScope@k_ZN10cmMak.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PushMacroScope@k_ZN10cmMak.body: The `PushMacroScope` helper records that a macro call has begun by taking a fresh snapshot of the current state. It then asserts that the snapshot is valid, pushes a defensive “barrier” to guard against re‑entering the same function block, and finally installs the supplied policy map into the new scope so that subsequent rendering honours the requested policy settings.

@lcmMakefile::PushPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefil.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PushPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefil.body: PushPolicy forwards a policy map and a weak‑flag to the internal StateSnapshot, which stores the policy in its own snapshot structure. This keeps the policy registration logic encapsulated within the snapshot handling layer, allowing the rest of the system to interact with policies only through the snapshot interface.

@lcmMakefile::PushScope@k_ZN10cmMakefile.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::PushScope@k_ZN10cmMakefile.body: PushScope creates a snapshot of the current variable scope by calling CreateVariableScopeSnapshot on the current state, then pushes a loop‑block barrier onto the stack. If the build is not running in a bootstrap environment (CMAKE_BOOTSTRAP not defined), it also pushes the current function scope onto the global file‑lock pool. The function then returns, leaving the new snapshot and barrier in place for the following parsing steps.

@lcmMakefile::RaiseScope@k_ZN10cmMakefil.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RaiseScope@k_ZN10cmMakefil.body: The method forwards the supplied key and value to an overload that accepts a C‑style string, passing `value.GetCStr()` as the argument.

@lcmMakefile::RaiseScope@k_ZN10cmMakefil.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RaiseScope@k_ZN10cmMakefil.body: The method first verifies the variable name isn’t empty, then delegates to the snapshot manager to set the variable’s scope. If the snapshot reports a failure (no parent scope available), it emits a warning and aborts. When boot‑strap mode is disabled, it also reports the change to any active variable‑watcher.

@lcmMakefile::RaiseScope@k_ZN10cmMakefil.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RaiseScope@k_ZN10cmMakefil.body: Iterates over the supplied variable names. For each name, it checks whether a normal definition already exists. If so, it calls the helper `RaiseScope` with that name and the existing definition. If not, it passes the name with a `nullptr`, effectively clearing that variable in the current scope.

@lcmMakefile::ReadDependentFile@k_ZN10cm.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ReadDependentFile@k_ZN10cm.body: The `ReadDependentFile` function resolves a filename relative to the current source directory, establishes a scoped include context, optionally notifies a debug adapter about the start and end of parsing, parses the list file into an internal representation, runs that file’s contents, and cleans up the include scope when a fatal error occurs, returning a success flag.

@lcmMakefile::ReadListFile@k_ZN10cmMakef.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ReadListFile@k_ZN10cmMakef.body: The function resolves a file path relative to the current source directory, creates a scoped guard for that file, and optionally notifies a debug adapter when parsing begins and ends. It then constructs a `cmListFile` object and parses the target file. If parsing fails, it informs the debug adapter, stops the scope, and returns `false`. Upon success it logs the successful parse, runs the parsed list file via `RunListFile`, and if any fatal error is triggered during that run it quiets the scope. Finally it returns `true` to indicate success.

@lcmMakefile::ReadListFileAsString@k_ZN1.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ReadListFileAsString@k_ZN1.body: The function resolves a virtual filename, initializes a scoped list‑file object, parses the supplied content string into that object, optionally reports success to a debug adapter, executes the parsed list file via `RunListFile`, and finally returns a success flag (false on parse failure or fatal error). It also ensures the scope is quietly cleaned up on fatal errors.

@lcmMakefile::RecordPolicies@k_ZNK10cmMa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RecordPolicies@k_ZNK10cmMa.body: Records the current status of every policy defined in the enumeration `cmPolicies` into the supplied `PolicyMap` by iterating over the policy IDs from `CMP0000` to `CMPCOUNT` and invoking `GetPolicyStatus` for each one.

@lcmMakefile::RemoveCacheDefinition@k_ZN.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RemoveCacheDefinition@k_ZN.body: The method simply forwards the cache‑name to the internal state object, invoking its `RemoveCacheEntry(name)` routine. It performs no further processing and returns immediately.

@lcmMakefile::RemoveDefineFlag@k_ZN10cmM.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RemoveDefineFlag@k_ZN10cmM.body: The function deletes a specified flag from the internal define‑flag collections of a cmMakefile instance. It first guards against an empty flag string, then calls an internal helper to erase the flag from the original definition list. If the flag isn’t recognised as a definition, it removes it from the standard define‑flag list instead.

@lcmMakefile::RemoveDefinition@k_ZN10cmM.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RemoveDefinition@k_ZN10cmM.body: The function deletes the named entry from the current make‑file state and, when the bootstrap flag is not defined, notifies any registered variable‑watcher that the variable was removed (calling VariableAccessed with VARIABLE_REMOVED_ACCESS).

@lcmMakefile::RemoveExportBuildFileGener.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RemoveExportBuildFileGener.body: The function searches the internal list for the supplied `cmExportBuildFileGenerator` instance and erases the corresponding entry when found.

@lcmMakefile::RemoveFunctionBlocker@k_ZN.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RemoveFunctionBlocker@k_ZN.body: The function pops the most recently added `cmFunctionBlocker` from the internal stack, returning it as a `std::unique_ptr`. It first asserts that at least one blocker exists and that the barriers stack remains consistent, then moves the top element out of the container, removes it, and hands the ownership back to the caller.

@lcmMakefile::RemoveVariablesInString@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RemoveVariablesInString@k_.body: The `RemoveVariablesInString` method scans the supplied string for variable‑style markers and deletes them in‑place. When `atOnly` is false, it strips occurrences of `${…}` and `$ENV{…}` placeholders using regex matches; it always removes `@…@` patterns as well. The method thus returns a string with all such variable tokens excised.

@lcmMakefile::RunListFile@k_ZN10cmMakefi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::RunListFile@k_ZN10cmMakefi.body: The `RunListFile` routine records the list file in its dependency list, temporarily swaps in the current and parent list‑file definitions, and then iterates over the functions stored in the parsed list file. During the loop it executes each function, monitors for fatal errors and a return command that may unwind the current scope, and after any deferred commands are processed it restores the original list‑file definitions. This keeps the internal state of the make‑file engine consistent across nested includes.

@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::ScopePushPop.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::ScopePushPop.body: The `ScopePushPop` constructor accepts a `cmMakefile*`, stores it in the `Makefile` member, and immediately calls `Makefile->PushScope()` to push a new scope onto the file’s internal stack. When the `ScopePushPop` instance goes out of scope, its destructor automatically pops that scope, ensuring the makefile’s scope stack is restored to its previous state.

@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::ScopePushPop.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::ScopePushPop.body: A `ScopePushPop` object represents a scope‐guard that pushes a scope when constructed and guarantees it is popped when the object is destroyed. To avoid accidental duplication of that guard (which could leave dangling scopes in the stack), the copy constructor is explicitly deleted, ensuring only one instance can own the push/pop lifecycle.

@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::operator=@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::operator=@k_.body: The deleted assignment operator prevents an instance from being reassigned after construction, ensuring that any `ScopePushPop` object cannot be copied or reassigned to another instance, which helps preserve its intended RAII semantics and avoids accidental misuse.

@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::~ScopePushPo.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ScopePushPop::~ScopePushPo.body: Calls `PopScope()` on its internal `Makefile` member to unwind the last scope that was pushed.

@lcmMakefile::SetArgcArgv@k_ZN10cmMakefi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetArgcArgv@k_ZN10cmMakefi.body: The method stores the argument count as the definition `CMAKE_ARGC` and then iterates through the supplied vector, adding each element as a separate definition named `CMAKE_ARGV0`, `CMAKE_ARGV1`, … `CMAKE_ARGVn`. Each argument is registered via `AddDefinition`, and the code hints at marking the variable as used (the calls to `MarkVariableAsUsed` are currently commented out).

@lcmMakefile::SetCheckCMP0000@k_ZN10cmMa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetCheckCMP0000@k_ZN10cmMa.body: The method assigns the supplied boolean value to the internal `CheckCMP0000` flag, enabling or disabling the corresponding check.

@lcmMakefile::SetComplainRegularExpressi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetComplainRegularExpressi.body: The method stores the supplied regex pattern in the internal member used to filter file names that should trigger a complaint. It simply assigns the argument to the internal string field.

@lcmMakefile::SetGlobalTargetImportScope.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetGlobalTargetImportScope.body: The constructor checks whether the supplied `scope` equals `ImportedTargetScope::Global` and the current makefile is not already in a global scope. If both conditions hold, it records the new scope in `CurrentImportedTargetScope` and flags that a change has occurred (`Set = true`). If the scope is already global or the makefile is in a global scope, it leaves the flag unset (`Set = false`). This ensures the internal state reflects only a genuine transition to the global import mode.

@lcmMakefile::SetGlobalTargetImportScope.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetGlobalTargetImportScope.body: When the internal `Set` flag is true, the method assigns the `Makefile`’s `CurrentImportedTargetScope` field to the `ImportedTargetScope::Local` value.

@lcmMakefile::SetIncludeRegularExpressio.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetIncludeRegularExpressio.body: The method simply stores a supplied regex string as the value for a property named “INCLUDE_REGULAR_EXPRESSION” by delegating to the internal `SetProperty` helper. It performs no validation or parsing of the pattern, and the property name contains typographical errors (“INCLUDE” / “REGULAR”).

@lcmMakefile::SetPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefile.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefile.body: SetPolicy updates the policy status if the requested transition is valid. It verifies that a REQUIRED_ALWAYS policy can only be set to NEW, emits a fatal error if that rule is violated, emits a deprecation warning under specific conditions, then records the new status in the state snapshot.

@lcmMakefile::SetPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefile.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetPolicy@k_ZN10cmMakefile.body: It maps a string ID to an internal policy ID, emits a fatal error and returns false if the ID isn’t registered, otherwise delegates the status to the internal SetPolicy overload.

@lcmMakefile::SetPolicyVersion@k_ZN10cmM.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetPolicyVersion@k_ZN10cmM.body: The function delegates to `cmPolicies::ApplyPolicyVersion`, passing the provided minimum and maximum strings and requesting a warning‑on compatibility check, then returns that call’s Boolean result.

@lcmMakefile::SetProjectName@k_ZN10cmMak.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetProjectName@k_ZN10cmMak.body: Sets the project name in the internal state snapshot. The call simply forwards the supplied string to the `StateSnapshot` object, which stores it for later use. No validation or side‑effects are performed in this snippet; callers should handle any required checks.

@lcmMakefile::SetProperty@k_ZN10cmMakefi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetProperty@k_ZN10cmMakefi.body: This method forwards a property assignment to the current directory. It retrieves the directory from the state snapshot, then invokes that directory’s SetProperty with the supplied property name, value, and a back‑trace reference.

@lcmMakefile::SetProperty@k_ZN10cmMakefi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetProperty@k_ZN10cmMakefi.body: Convenient wrapper: forwards the call to the real overload, passing a `cmValue` initialized with `nullptr`.

@lcmMakefile::SetProperty@k_ZN10cmMakefi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetProperty@k_ZN10cmMakefi.body: This overload accepts a property name and a string value, wraps the value with a cmValue helper, and forwards the call to the underlying implementation of SetProperty.

@lcmMakefile::SetRecursionDepth@k_ZN10cm.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetRecursionDepth@k_ZN10cm.body: The function stores the supplied depth value in the object’s internal `RecursionDepth` field. It simply assigns the argument to the member; no validation or side‑effects are performed.

@lcmMakefile::SetScriptModeFile@k_ZN10cm.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::SetScriptModeFile@k_ZN10cm.body: The method stores the supplied script file name under the key `CMAKE_SCRIPT_MODE_FILE` in the makefile’s definition table, enabling downstream code to recognize the file as the script mode source.

@lcmMakefile::StoreMatches@k_ZN10cmMakef.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::StoreMatches@k_ZN10cmMakef.body: The function iterates over the first ten matches of a supplied regular expression. For each non‑empty match it records the matched text in the current context by adding a definition for the corresponding variable, marks that variable as used, and records the highest‑indexed match seen. After the loop it stores the highest index in a single‑character string and records that as a definition as well.

@lcmMakefile::TryCompile@k_ZN10cmMakefil.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::TryCompile@k_ZN10cmMakefil.body: The method orchestrates a test‑build by preparing the working directory, configuring a CMake generator instance (including any supplied CLI arguments and build‑type settings), running the generator’s configure and generate passes, and finally invoking that generator’s `TryCompile` method. It reports fatal errors and sets internal flags for the try‑compile state, returning the generator’s status code.

@lcmMakefile::ValidateCustomCommand@k_ZN.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::ValidateCustomCommand@k_ZN.body: The `ValidateCustomCommand` routine scans each command line in the supplied list. If a non‑empty line begins with a literal quote character it records a fatal error message and immediately returns `false`; otherwise the function completes successfully and returns `true`.

@lcmMakefile::VariableInitialized@k_ZNK1.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::VariableInitialized@k_ZNK1.body: It checks the internal snapshot for the variable’s initialization flag.

@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::VariableP.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::VariableP.body:
Initialises a `VariablePushPop` instance by storing the supplied `cmMakefile` reference in the `Makefile` member.  
Immediately after that, it updates the internal `StateSnapshot` with a freshly‑created snapshot that represents the current variable scope at that point in the script.  
This effectively pushes the current variable scope onto an internal stack, allowing later restoration or rollback of that snapshot.

@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::VariableP.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::VariableP.body: This helper class automatically registers a variable in a context when created and unregisters it when destroyed, effectively giving a push‑on‑construction / pop‑on‑destruction scope guard for variable handling.

@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::operator=.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::operator=.body: The deleted assignment operator prevents copying or assigning a `VariablePushPop` instance; any attempt to use `obj1 = obj2` results in a compile‑time error.

@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::~Variable.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::VariablePushPop::~Variable.body: The destructor `VariablePushPop::~VariablePushPop()` simply invokes `Makefile->PopSnapshot()` to revert any temporary state changes made during the lifetime of a `VariablePushPop` instance, ensuring that when the object is destroyed its snapshot is removed and the surrounding environment is restored to its original state.

@lcmMakefile::cmMakefile@k_ZN10cmMakefil.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::cmMakefile@k_ZN10cmMakefil.body: The constructor stores the supplied global generator and state snapshot, initializes internal flags (e.g., `IsSourceFileTryCompile`, `SuppressSideEffects`, and `CheckCMP0000`), and compiles regular‑expressions for parsing `cmakedefine` directives, variable references (`@…@`), and source names. It then creates a policy‑scope snapshot from the current snapshot, pushes the policy level for the current directory, and pushes an empty loop‑block barrier. Finally it registers source groups for source files, headers, PCH files, rule files, resources, and object libraries—adding an extra “Object Libraries” group when the `CMAKE_BOOTSTRAP` macro is not defined.

@lcmMakefile::cmMakefile@k_ZN10cmMakefil.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::cmMakefile@k_ZN10cmMakefil.body: The deleted copy constructor prevents accidental copying of a cmMakefile instance, ensuring that only explicit construction (or moving) is allowed.

@lcmMakefile::operator=@k_ZN10cmMakefile.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::operator=@k_ZN10cmMakefile.body: The deleted assignment operator stops any attempt to copy‑assign a `cmMakefile` instance, ensuring the object can’t be replaced after construction.

@lcmMakefile::~cmMakefile@k_ZN10cmMakefi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefile::~cmMakefile@k_ZN10cmMakefi.body: The destructor `~cmMakefile` is called when a `cmMakefile` instance goes out of scope; it releases any internally allocated resources and cleans up the internal state of the object.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.body: The method produces a makefile rule that links the compiled CUDA device code into an executable only when the target requires device linking. It gathers the output name from the “CMAKE_CUDA_OUTPUT_EXTENSION” definition, increments a progress counter, optionally prints a progress message, then dispatches to the appropriate linker (Clang‑style or NVIDIA‑style) depending on the compiler ID. Finally it writes the top‑level driver rule that builds the whole target.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.body: Creates the Makefile rule that will build an executable target. It sets up the output paths, assembles link flags and dependencies, and emits the sequence of shell commands (including optional link‑script invocation) needed to link the final binary, handling pre‑/post‑build hooks, import‑library handling, symlink creation and cleanup.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.body: The function builds a link rule for a CUDA‑device executable: it collects all device‑specific dependencies, assembles the appropriate compiler and linker flags (including any response‑file handling), and then emits the make rule—optionally using a link script to keep command lines short. Once the rule is written, it records the executable’s cleanup list so that the build system can delete temporary artefacts.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::W.body: The routine drives the entire makefile generation for an executable target. It first opens the file with CreateRuleFile(), then emits shared build rules (common code, target‑specific flags, and object‑file handling). After that it emits the device‑specific link and general executable linking rules, adds any extra relink step needed for an installable copy, and writes the dependency rules that tie targets together. Finally, it writes the cleanup rule and closes the output streams.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::c.body: The constructor initializes a make‑file target generator for an executable target. It stores the target’s executable names derived from the current configuration, records a custom command driver (``OnDepends``), and creates an ``cmOSXBundleGenerator`` instance. It also supplies this generator with a reference to the list of macOS content folders that will be used later for bundle generation.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::c.body: The constructor copies the internal state from an existing `cmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator` instance, initializing the new object’s internal generator data so it can immediately start producing executable target rules in a Makefile.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::o.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::o.body: The assignment operator copies the internal state from the right‑hand operand into the current instance and returns a reference to the object itself for chaining.

@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::~.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator::~.body: When an instance of **cmMakefileExecutableTargetGenerator** is destroyed, its destructor performs the cleanup work required for that object. It releases any resources that were acquired during the object’s lifetime—such as deallocating internally‑allocated memory or closing file handles—and it calls any base‑class destructors it inherits. In short, it guarantees that the object’s internal state is cleanly torn down before the object is reclaimed.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: The method orchestrates the generation of a makefile rule that links a device‑specific library. It first builds the output filename (`cmake_device_link.<ext>`), records it in `DeviceLinkObject`, and increments an internal progress counter. If messages are enabled, it emits an echo describing the linking step. Depending on the compiler ID it either writes the standard clang rule via `WriteDeviceLinkRule` or emits the Nvidia‑specific rules via `WriteNvidiaDeviceLibraryRules`. Finally it appends the resulting commands to the main driver rule with `WriteTargetDriverRule`.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: This function resolves the linker language for the current configuration, builds a variable name for the framework‑creation rule, collects any target‑specific flags, registers those flags under the appropriate CMake configuration variable, and finally invokes `WriteLibraryRules` to emit the corresponding Makefile rules for the framework target.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: The routine builds the make‑file rule that produces a library. It collects the required objects and libraries, computes the needed flags (including Apple‑specific framework options), sets up the proper output paths, and emits the linking commands—optionally using response files or a link script. It also arranges the necessary cleanup entries for the generated files.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: The routine prepares the linker command for a module target. It first determines whether device‑linking is needed; if so it emits that specific rule. It then pulls the appropriate linker language, collects the target’s extra flags, and builds a `cmLinkLineComputer` for the current configuration. Finally, it augments the flag list with the module‑definition flag and writes the final linker rule for that target.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: The function constructs the makefile rules needed to link a CUDA‑target library, gathering its dependencies, applying the appropriate compiler flags, handling response files and possible link‑script invocation, and finally inserting the resulting rule into the target’s makefile stream.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: This helper collates the commands and dependency list for the library target, passes them to the local generator to emit the make rule that builds the objects, and then registers a driver rule for the target.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: The routine orchestrates the generation of all the make‑file fragments that back a build target. It first creates the rule file, writes shared code blocks, then emits per‑target flags and build rules for objects and custom commands. After that it emits the link‑dependency rules and finally writes the specific link rules for the target’s type—static, shared, module, or object library—handling re‑linking for installable targets. It finishes with a clean‑up rule, the dependency‑generation rule, and then closes the streams.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body:
The routine emits the make rules for a shared‑library target.  
If the target is an Apple‑style framework it delegates to the framework writer; otherwise, when not relinking, it may emit device‑linker rules. It then figures out the linker language, constructs the appropriate linker variable name, gathers any extra flags (including module definitions and LWYU handling), and finally writes the rule that invokes the linker to create the shared library.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::Writ.body: The method checks whether device‑linking is required for the target; if so it emits the corresponding device rules. It then queries the target’s linker language, derives the appropriate rule variable, gathers any extra compiler flags, and finally writes out the library build rules using that information.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::cmMa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::cmMa.body: The constructor creates a library‑target generator: it registers itself with the base generator, sets the custom command driver to “OnDepends”, collects the library names unless the target is an interface library, and finally creates a unique OS X bundle generator that receives the content‑folder list.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::cmMa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::cmMa.body: The `cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator` function creates a new library target by copying the configuration from an existing `cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator` instance, populating the target’s properties (such as sources, include directories, and link flags), and registering it with the build system.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::oper.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::oper.body: The `operator=` function performs a deep copy of another `cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator` instance into the current object, reinitializing all of its internal data members (including inherited state from `cmMakefileTargetGenerator`) to mirror the source’s configuration. It returns a reference to the modified object so that chained assignments can be performed.

@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::~cmM.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator::~cmM.body: The destructor of `cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenerator` performs the necessary clean‑up for a library‑target generator: it releases any allocated resources, removes registered callbacks, and ensures that any derived‑class specific finalisation steps are executed before the object is reclaimed.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.body: This constructor adopts the resource owned by *other* into the new instance. It copies the `Data` pointer from `other` to the current object, then resets `other.Data` to `nullptr` so the source instance no longer owns the resource. The operation is marked `noexcept` to guarantee it cannot throw during the transfer.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.body: RAII is a public member that explicitly deletes the copy‑constructor (`RAII(const RAII&) = delete;`). By marking the copy constructor as deleted, the class can’t be copied – any attempt to copy an instance will be a compile‑time error. This guarantees that objects of the class maintain unique ownership and cannot be inadvertently duplicated.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.body: RAII creates a profiling entry for a specified category and name, forwarding any optional arguments into the underlying `StartEntry` call.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::RAII@k_.body: RAII is a function that performs a delete operation, typically invoked to free or remove data structures in the code.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::operato.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::operato.body: The move‐assignment operator first destroys the current data (calling `StopEntry()` on the stored pointer if it exists), then transfers ownership of the incoming object’s data pointer to the current instance while setting the source’s pointer to `nullptr`.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::operato.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::operato.body:
The `operator=` declaration deletes the copy‑assignment operator for `RAII`.  
That means you **cannot assign** one `RAII` instance to another (e.g., `a = b;` will be a compile‑time error). This prevents accidental reassignment and enforces immutability of `RAII` objects.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::~RAII@k.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::RAII::~RAII@k.body: This destructor stops the profiling entry if the internal data object exists, calling `StopEntry()` on that data before the object is destroyed.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::StartEntry@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::StartEntry@k_.body: The function serializes a profiling event into a JSON record and writes it to a shared output stream. It appends a comma separator between successive entries, populates a fixed set of fields—phase flag, event name, category tag, current timestamp, process ID and a zero thread ID—and, when supplied, includes the optional arguments map. The write operation is wrapped in a try‑catch that logs any output failure.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::StopEntry@k_Z.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::StopEntry@k_Z.body: When called, StopEntry appends a comma to the profiling output stream, builds a JSON event record containing a phase marker (“E”) and a timestamp in microseconds along with the current process ID (thread ID is hard‑coded to 0), and writes the record to the stream via the JsonWriter. Any stream‑write exception is caught and logged; a fatal exception simply reports a generic error.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::cmMakefilePro.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::cmMakefilePro.body: The constructor opens a file named by the supplied path, creates a JSON stream writer via a builder, and writes the opening “[” character to that stream. If the file cannot be opened, it throws a `std::runtime_error`.

@lcmMakefileProfilingData::~cmMakefilePr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileProfilingData::~cmMakefilePr.body: Closes the profiling output stream: when the profiling session ends, the destructor writes a closing delimiter to the stream, then attempts to close the stream while swallowing any exceptions that might arise during the write or close operation.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AddIncludeF.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AddIncludeF.body: It collects the include‑directory list for the target’s language and builds the compiler‑flag string that lists those directories. It then queries a CMake‑specific variable to see if a response file should be used; if so, it writes the flag list to a .rsp file and appends the resulting path flag to the output string; otherwise it appends the raw flag string directly. The routine relies on Makefile, LocalGenerator, and FlagFileDepends to obtain and store the flags.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AppendLinkD.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AppendLinkD.body: Collects all prerequisites required before a link operation: it pulls in object files, target prerequisites, module definition sources, manifest files, and any user‑supplied link dependencies into the dependency list.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AppendObjec.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AppendObjec.body: The routine builds the full list of prerequisite files for a makefile target. It collects the relative paths of every object file produced in this build pass, appends them to the supplied vector, then merges in any external object files, and finally records the rule‑specific build‑file itself as a dependency.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AppendTarge.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::AppendTarge.body: The routine walks the generator’s dependency list and appends any files that the target actually needs. It first short‑circuits static libraries unless a flag forces it; then it looks up the target’s current configuration. If the target declares a link‑dependency file, it pushes that path onto the list. Finally it pulls the stored link information for the target and merges that set of prerequisites into the list.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CheckUseRes.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CheckUseRes.body: The function probes the makefile for a variable named `CMAKE_<library>_USE_RESPONSE_FILE_FOR_LIBRARIES`. If that definition exists and contains a non‑empty value, it interprets the value with `cmIsOn`; otherwise it defaults to `false`.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CheckUseRes.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CheckUseRes.body: The function checks whether object files should be passed via a response file. It first looks for a “CMAKE_<target>_USE_RESPONSE_FILE_FOR_OBJECTS” definition; if that is present and set to “ON”, it returns true. If not, it computes the combined length of all object paths, and if that exceeds half the system’s command‑line limit it decides a response file is needed, otherwise it does not.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CloseFileSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CloseFileSt.body: The method simply releases three stream objects used by the target generator. It calls `reset()` on each of the `BuildFileStream`, `InfoFileStream`, and `FlagFileStream` members, which clears the internal pointers and frees the associated resources. This ensures the generator no longer holds open file streams once it finishes building a target.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateLinkL.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateLinkL.body: The method assembles a single string containing all libraries that must be linked, optionally writing that list to a response‑file when the “useResponseFile” flag is true. It first obtains link‑information via the target generator, then calls the local generator to build the list of library paths, prefixing them with the framework and link paths. If a response file is requested, the helper builds a file containing the list, records the file in the dependency list, and finally prefixes that file reference (via a response‑flag) to the library list. The result is left in the `linkLibs` argument; the function itself produces no return value.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateLinkL.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateLinkL.body: Creates a unique‑pointer to a link‑line computer. It checks whether the current Makefile is for MSVC 60; if so, it delegates to `GlobalGenerator->CreateMSVC60LinkLineComputer`, otherwise it calls `GlobalGenerator->CreateLinkLineComputer`. The returned object is then used to generate link‑line output during build generation.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateLinkS.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateLinkS.body: The routine generates a temporary script containing the supplied link commands and registers a makefile entry that runs that script. It writes the commands to a file in the target build directory (skipping empty or “:”‑prefixed lines), then appends a command to the makefile that invokes the script with the appropriate arguments and records the script path as a dependency for the target.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateObjec.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateObjec.body: The function builds the list of object‑file names that will later be linked. It writes that list into a variable (or into a response file when the target compiler needs it), taking care to quote names properly, and finally sets the build‑string that will be passed to the link stage. It handles the three modes (plain link, response‑file, or script) and returns the string that contains the references to all object files for the current rule.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateRespo.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateRespo.body: The function creates a response file containing the command‑line options. It first picks an encoding heuristically (UTF‑8 with BOM, dropping the BOM when the tool isn’t MSVC‑compatible), then writes the options string to the file. The full path of the new file is added to the supplied dependency list, and the relative path (inside the target’s build directory) is returned for later use.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateRuleF.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::CreateRuleF.body: It creates a rule file for a target: it resolves the target directory, builds the full file names, opens a stream with copy‑if‑different semantics, writes a disclaimer and the special‑targets header, and if the global flag allows it, emits a delete‑on‑error rule.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::DriveCustom.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::DriveCustom.body: Appends the list of outputs produced by the custom command to the supplied dependency vector, ensuring those outputs become part of the target’s dependency list.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GenDefFile@.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GenDefFile@.body: The routine first checks that a def‑file is enabled for the current target. If it is, it builds a CMake command line that invokes the `__create_def` helper, pointing it at the target’s def file and a temporary “.objs” list file. It then injects that command at the front of the link‑command vector. Finally it writes the list file containing all object files (including special handling for Windows‑export‑all cases) and the source paths that the def‑generator must read.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GenerateCus.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GenerateCus.body: The function collects a custom command’s comment and command list, writes the corresponding Makefile rule (with outputs, dependencies, and commands), manages implicit dependencies and symbolic input handling, and updates the global rule‑hash cache.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GenerateExt.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GenerateExt.body: The protected `GenerateExtraOutput` method accepts two C‑style strings—`out` and `in`—typically representing file paths or command strings. Within the code base it is invoked in several modules (e.g., the target generator in `cmMakefileTargetGenerator.h`). Its primary job is to write an auxiliary output artifact based on the supplied strings: it parses the source input, formats the appropriate target metadata, and appends the result into the designated output file. Because the parameters are raw pointers, callers must guard against null pointers and ensure the strings are null‑terminated; otherwise the routine may attempt to write past memory bounds. The function usually performs a straightforward stream‑write operation, so performance is dominated by I/O latency rather than in‑memory computation, and it should be wrapped in a try‑catch or error‑code return if the file system reports any failure.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetClangTid.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetClangTid.body: The function builds the full path to the file that will hold clang‑tidy replacement data for a given source file. It takes the target directory and the source file, obtains the object name via the generator, then constructs a relative path inside the build‑tree (using the current binary directory and the target’s own directory) and finally collapses that path into a canonical absolute path. The returned string is that resolved file path.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetConfigNa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetConfigNa.body: The function retrieves the single configuration name that the current generator expects. It calls `GetConfigNames()` on the `LocalGenerator`, verifies that exactly one name is present (via `assert`), and then returns that lone entry.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetDeviceLi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetDeviceLi.body: The routine pulls the link options for the current build configuration from the target and local generator objects, then appends those options to the supplied linkFlags string. While doing so it turns on the link‑script shell for the duration of the operation and turns it off afterward.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetGenerato.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetGenerato.body: It exposes the class’s internal `GeneratorTarget` pointer to callers. The method returns that pointer unchanged, so callers obtain direct access to the target object without copying. It contains no side‑effects, and it does not modify any internal state. Because the return type is a raw pointer, callers must handle potential `nullptr` and must not take ownership of the returned resource. This accessor is not marked `const`, so it could theoretically be called from a non‑`const` context; it does not, however, alter any state.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetLinkRule.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetLinkRule.body: The routine pulls a link‑rule string from the makefile, optionally extending it with a special “GNU‑to‑MS” suffix when the current build configuration requires a GNU‑to‑MS linker adaptation. It returns the final rule string.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetNumberOf.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetNumberOf.body: The function is an overridden virtual member that simply returns the private member `NumberOfProgressActions`. It retrieves and returns the stored count of progress actions without any additional processing.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetProgress.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetProgress.body: The member function returns the stored value of `ProgressFileNameFull`, giving the full path or name of the progress file.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetResponse.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetResponse.body: The function retrieves a string flag value used in Makefile generation. It chooses a flag variable name based on the requested link type (normal link or device‑link). It looks up that variable in the current Makefile’s definitions; if defined, the retrieved value replaces the default “@”. The returned string is the flag that will be inserted into the generated Makefile commands.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetTargetLi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::GetTargetLi.body: The method collects and appends link‑time flags for a target. It pulls the default “LINK_FLAGS” property from the target, then fetches a configuration‑specific value (e.g., “LINK_FLAGS_<CONFIG>”), adds any link options from the target for the current configuration, temporarily enables the link‑script shell to escape compile options, and finally appends both position‑independent and dependency‑info flags.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.body: The move‑constructor of `MacOSXContentGeneratorType` takes an rvalue reference (`&&`) to another instance and re‑initializes the current object with that instance’s resources, ensuring that any owned data is transferred rather than copied. This pattern is typically used to implement efficient ownership transfer for objects that manage non‑copyable resources.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.body: The constructor simply stores the supplied `cmMakefileTargetGenerator` pointer in the `Generator` member; no further setup logic is performed.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.body: The declaration defines a copy‑constructor for the `MacOSXContentGeneratorType` struct. When invoked, it creates a new instance that duplicates the state of an existing one, enabling the object to be passed or returned without altering the source.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.body: When the build target is a bundle, the method determines the bundle’s content directory, records the source file to be copied, and appends a copy rule to the makefile so that file ends up in the final bundle.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.body: This overload takes an r‑value of the same type, moves its contents into the target object, and returns a reference to the modified object so callers can chain assignments. It performs a move‑assignment, avoiding deep copies while preserving correct state after the operation.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.body: The assignment operator copies the internal state of the source `MacOSXContentGeneratorType` into the target instance and returns a reference to the target, enabling chained assignments while preserving the generator’s internal configuration.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MacOSXConte.body: The ~MacOSXContentGeneratorType() virtual function is the hook that a subclass implements to provide the specific “Content” string that the make‑file generator emits for a Mac OS X target. When called, the function is expected to return a string (or a structured object) that encodes the macro‑expanded content that should be inserted into the generated makefile. In practice, a concrete implementation typically concatenates the target’s configuration details—such as SDK paths, compiler flags, and any custom build‑time options—into a single string that is then written out by the cmMakefileTargetGenerator during the .makefile generation phase.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MakeEchoPro.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::MakeEchoPro.body: The function prepares an `EchoProgress` object for a CMake make‑file run. It populates the `Dir` field with the binary directory plus a “/CMakeFiles” suffix and builds the `Arg` field with the string `$(CMAKE_PROGRESS_<number>)` where `<number>` comes from the generator’s `NumberOfProgressActions`.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::New@k_ZN25c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::New@k_ZN25c.body: The function examines the target’s type via `GetType()` and, using a `switch`, constructs an instance of the appropriate concrete generator (`Executable`, `Library`, or `Utility`). It creates that object with `make_unique`, stores it in a `unique_ptr`, and finally returns it. If the type isn’t one of the handled cases, the function returns a null‑owned pointer.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteCommon.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteCommon.body: The routine builds the target’s dependency and flag macros: it emits the include directives for the target’s normal, compiler‑generated, and linker‑generated dependency files, writes empty placeholder files when no real deps exist, removes legacy internal files, and finally writes the progress and flag files into the makefile stream so the generated build knows where to read its compile flags and progress state.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteDevice.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteDevice.body: The routine builds the make‑file rules for compiling and linking the CUDA device‑side code. It first validates that CUDA architecture flags are set, then gathers all required link dependencies (including built objects and device‑specific files). For each requested compute capability it emits a rule that invokes the device‑linker to produce a fat‑binary, registers the kernels, and collects the resulting cubin files. Finally it writes a rule that combines those binaries into a single fat‑binary image, generates a stub that performs the register step, and cleans up temporary artifacts.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteMakeRu.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteMakeRu.body: The function generates a make rule for a target that may produce one or many files. It first writes a rule for the first output (marking it symbolic if needed), then, if there are extra outputs, it adds rules that make each of those depend on the first and optionally creates a “touch” placeholder so *make* sees them as up‑to‑date. The function returns whether any of the outputs were symbolic.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.body: This routine builds a list of prerequisites for an object build. It first records the source file’s own path, then checks for an “OBJECT_DEPENDS” property; if present, it expands that list into the dependency vector.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.body: The routine registers a source file’s translation into an object file. It detects the file’s language, decides whether compiler‑generated dependency data is required, and records the object file to avoid duplicate rules. It then emits the compilation command (including flags, defines, include dirs, and any PCH/header handling), records implicit dependencies, and writes the corresponding rule into the build file. If pre‑processing or assembly is required for the language, it emits the associated preprocessor/assembly rules and cleans up any extra output files.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.body: Builds a list of object file names for the target. It skips any files ending in the current PCH extension, feeds the remaining objects, external objects, and any implicitly‑generated ISPC objects into a helper object that serialises them into the supplied vector, and then signals completion with helper.Done().

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteObject.body: Creates two make‑file variables for the target: one holding the ordinary object files, the other holding external objects. It writes comment headers, generates the variable names via the local generator, and dumps the quoted file paths into the build‑file stream, respecting line‑continuation and skipping any PCH files.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteRuleFi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteRuleFi.body: The `WriteRuleFiles` pure virtual member is intended to be overridden by concrete subclasses to emit the rule‑definition files needed by the build system. In practice a derived class implements it to serialize its internal rule data (targets, dependencies, custom commands, etc.) into the appropriate output format—generally XML/JSON rule files—or directly into the makefile. The base class merely declares the requirement; the actual file‑generation logic resides in the concrete subclasses that know the specific rule syntax for the target type.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.body: The routine assembles the build rules for a target: it verifies module status, registers and collects clean‑up files, emits custom‑command rules (including any ISPC extras), gathers object sources, and finally validates that all required source languages are enabled before generating the object‑rule files.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.body: The function creates a “clean” make‑rule that removes all files generated for a given target. It builds the target name in the target‑directory, collects the commands needed to delete those files (via `AppendCleanCommand` and a `cd` command to the binary directory), then emits the rule into the makefile stream.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.body: The routine produces a “DependInfo.cmake” file that records the target’s output files, their inter‑target links, and any Fortran‑specific flags, and then emits a make rule whose sole job is to invoke the CMake scanner (`cmake_depends`) to regenerate the dependency lists after a build.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.body: The function generates a makefile rule that drives the build of a target’s outputs. Depending on the *relink* flag it writes either a pre‑install relinking rule or a normal build rule, optionally ensuring custom command outputs and extra files are built first.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.body: The method enumerates every language that the current target supports, writes the compiler name and its associated flag definitions into the flag‑generation stream, and finally records the architecture‑specific flag strings while escaping any ‘#’ characters that would otherwise terminate the assignment.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::WriteTarget.body: The function first verifies whether the current target has an associated link‑dependency file. If none exists, it exits immediately. When a dependency file is present, it is fetched via the local generator, added to the list of files to be cleaned afterward, and finally registered as an implicit “LINK” dependency for the target so that the dependency scanner treats it as a compiler‑generated dependency.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::cmMakefileT.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::cmMakefileT.body: The constructor initializes the target generator by linking the target’s local and global generators, configuring command‑driver behavior, and setting internal flags according to global properties. It loads the “RULE_MESSAGES” property to decide whether to suppress rule‑related messages, then interprets the target’s policy status (WARN, OLD, NEW, REQUIRED…​) to set the `CMP0113New` flag accordingly. Finally, it creates a content generator instance that will later produce the makefile fragments.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::cmMakefileT.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::cmMakefileT.body: Prevents copying of a cmMakefileTargetGenerator instance – the deleted copy‑constructor guarantees that any attempt to copy such an object fails at compile time.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::operator=@k.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::operator=@k.body: The assignment operator takes a source object, copies its internal state into the current instance (typically via member‑wise copy or a copy‑constructor‑style implementation) and then returns a reference to `*this`. This enables code to use the familiar `=` syntax for copying a `cmMakefileTargetGenerator` object.

@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::~cmMakefile.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileTargetGenerator::~cmMakefile.body: A virtual destructor (`~cmMakefileTargetGenerator`) is declared so that derived classes can override it. It ensures that when a `cmMakefileTargetGenerator` object is deleted through a base‑pointer, the derived destructor runs, cleaning up resources in the correct subclass. The implementation in the source file simply provides the default destructor (`=default`), so no custom cleanup logic is needed unless a subclass supplies its own override.

@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::Writ.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::Writ.body: The routine orchestrates the creation of a rule‑file for a CMake target: it starts by generating a bare rule file, appends a comment header, and then pulls in custom‑command dependencies. It collects and emits the pre‑/post‑build command streams, appends those to the rule file, and finally writes out the rule, driver, clean, and dependency‑generation rules before flushing the file streams.

@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::cmMa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::cmMa.body: Creates a utility‑target helper that stores a reference to its owning target. It assigns the command driver flag to “OnUtility”, instantiates an OS X bundle generator tied to the target, and wires that generator to the helper’s `MacContentFolders` list.

@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::cmMa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::cmMa.body:
`cmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator` is the copy‑constructor for the target‑generation helper.  
It clones the internal state of an existing generator instance so that the new object inherits all the necessary context (e.g., target‑specific options, helper flags, and file‑path info) to produce a fresh but otherwise identical output target.

@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::oper.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::oper.body: The `operator=` member copies all internal state from another `cmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator` into the current instance, delegating to the base class’s assignment when appropriate, and then returns `*this`.

@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::~cmM.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator::~cmM.body: The destructor `~cmMakefileUtilityTargetGenerator()` is responsible for cleaning up the state of a target‑generation utility: it shuts down any open file descriptors, frees allocated buffers, and releases internal data structures that were used while generating makefile targets. This guarantees that any temporary resources are released when the object is destroyed.

@lcmMarkAsAdvancedCommand@k_Z23cmMarkAsA.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMarkAsAdvancedCommand@k_Z23cmMarkAsA.body: The function parses a list of cache variable names. If the first argument is “CLEAR” or “FORCE”, it clears or forces the entry, setting a flag that the variable should be overwritten. It then checks the current CMP0102 policy: under WARN it emits a warning if the variable is missing; under OLD it creates a dummy cache entry; under NEW it may ignore the variable if unset. Finally, for each variable that remains, it ensures a cache entry exists and sets the “ADVANCED” property to “1” (or “0” when cleared) as appropriate, marking it as advanced.

@lcmMathCommand@k_Z13cmMathCommandRKiR17.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMathCommand@k_Z13cmMathCommandRKiR17.body: The function receives a list of arguments, verifies that at least one is present, then inspects the first token. If that token equals "EXPR" it forwards control to a dedicated handler; any other token triggers an error response. The function reports its success or failure via the status object.

@lcmMessageCommand@k_Z16cmMessageCommand.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessageCommand@k_Z16cmMessageCommand.body: The function interprets a command vector to determine a message’s type, severity level, and any special handling flags. It performs a series of checks against the first argument to set flags such as fatal error, warning, author warning, or status reporting modes, and configures the appropriate log level. Once the level is established, it concatenates the remaining arguments into a single message string and routes that string to the relevant output routine (standard log, status display, or specialized status check handling). If a fatal flag is set, it records a fatal error event before returning. If the message level is suppressed by current settings, the function exits early without output.

@lcmMessageMetadata::cmMessageMetadata@k.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessageMetadata::cmMessageMetadata@k.body: The function gathers message‑level metadata (e.g., sender, subject, timestamps, flags) into a structured form for later use in processing or logging. It returns this composite data to callers that need it for routing, persistence, or audit purposes.

@lcmMessenger::ConvertMessageType@k_ZNK1.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::ConvertMessageType@k_ZNK1.body: The function maps a requested message type to the appropriate internal type according to the current configuration: if the input is an author warning or error, it returns the error type when “developer warnings as errors” is enabled; otherwise it keeps a warning. The same logic applies to deprecation messages, returning the error form when “deprecated warnings as errors” is enabled. In all other cases, it simply passes the type through unchanged.

@lcmMessenger::DisplayMessage@k_ZNK11cmM.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::DisplayMessage@k_ZNK11cmM.body: Creates a message string from the message type and supplied text, optionally appending the back‑trace information, then shows it (via the messenger’s display routine). If a debugger adapter is attached, the message is also forwarded to that component.

@lcmMessenger::GetDeprecatedWarningsAsEr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::GetDeprecatedWarningsAsEr.body: Returns the value of the internal flag `DeprecatedWarningsAsErrors`, indicating whether the system should treat deprecation warnings as errors.

@lcmMessenger::GetDevWarningsAsErrors@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::GetDevWarningsAsErrors@k_.body: The function returns the value of the member variable `DevWarningsAsErrors`. It is a simple const getter that does nothing more than exposing that boolean flag.

@lcmMessenger::GetSuppressDeprecatedWarn.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::GetSuppressDeprecatedWarn.body: The method simply returns the value of the member flag `SuppressDeprecatedWarnings`. Because it is marked `const`, callers are guaranteed that invoking it will not modify the object state, and the return type (`bool`) is an immutable value copy of the stored flag.

@lcmMessenger::GetSuppressDevWarnings@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::GetSuppressDevWarnings@k_.body: Returns the internal `SuppressDevWarnings` flag, indicating whether developer‑level warnings are turned off.

@lcmMessenger::IsMessageTypeVisible@k_ZN.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::IsMessageTypeVisible@k_ZN.body: The function simply decides whether a message should be shown based on the current settings. For a *DEPRECATION_ERROR* it shows the message only if deprecated warnings are treated as errors. A *DEPRECATION_WARNING* is shown only when the system is not configured to suppress deprecated warnings. An *AUTHOR_ERROR* is visible only when developer‑level warnings are treated as errors, and an *AUTHOR_WARNING* is visible only when developer‑level warnings are not suppressed. All other message types are considered visible by default.

@lcmMessenger::IssueMessage@k_ZNK11cmMes.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::IssueMessage@k_ZNK11cmMes.body: The routine rewrites the supplied message type via `ConvertMessageType`. If the conversion alters the type, it forces the new type; otherwise it retains the original. When the (possibly new) type is visible—either naturally or by the forced flag—it forwards the text and back‑trace to `DisplayMessage`.

@lcmMessenger::PrintBacktraceTitle@k_ZNK.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::PrintBacktraceTitle@k_ZNK.body:
The routine formats a concise, human‑readable location for a file backtrace:  
– if the trace list is empty it exits without output,  
– it pulls the top entry, normalises the path relative to the base source (when available),  
– and writes “in …​” for a file‑only reference or “at …​” when a line number is present.

@lcmMessenger::SetTopSource@k_ZN11cmMess.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmMessenger::SetTopSource@k_ZN11cmMess.body: Sets the `TopSource` member to the supplied optional string, using move‑semantics to avoid copies.

@lcmNewLineStyle::GetCharacters@k_ZNK14c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::GetCharacters@k_ZNK14c.body: The function returns a string literal that represents the newline sequence used by the current `NewLineStyle`. When the style is `Invalid` it yields an empty string; for `LF` it returns a single “\n”, and for `CRLF` it returns “\r\n”. The final `return ""` is effectively unreachable because every `case` already returns.

@lcmNewLineStyle::GetStyle@k_ZNK14cmNewL.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::GetStyle@k_ZNK14cmNewL.body: The method returns the value stored in the member variable `NewLineStyle`, providing read‑only access to that style object.

@lcmNewLineStyle::IsValid@k_ZNK14cmNewLi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::IsValid@k_ZNK14cmNewLi.body: It returns true when the member `NewLineStyle` holds a value other than the sentinel value `Invalid`.

@lcmNewLineStyle::ReadFromArguments@k_ZN.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::ReadFromArguments@k_ZN.body: This function iterates over a vector of command‑line tokens to locate a `"NEWLINE_STYLE"` flag. When it finds the flag, it expects the following token to specify a supported line‑ending style (`LF`, `CRLF`, `UNIX`, `DOS`, or `WIN32`). It sets the internal `NewLineStyle` enum accordingly and reports success. If the expected token is missing or unrecognised, it assigns an error message to `errorString` and returns `false`.

@lcmNewLineStyle::SetStyle@k_ZN14cmNewLi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::SetStyle@k_ZN14cmNewLi.body: The method assigns the supplied `Style` value to the instance’s internal `NewLineStyle` field, making that value available for subsequent operations.

@lcmNewLineStyle::cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14c.body: Creates a new line‑style instance from the supplied parameters and returns a reference to the created object.

@lcmNewLineStyle::cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14c.body: cmNewLineStyle constructs a new line‑style object by copying an existing style instance (or default values when none is supplied) and returns that instance. It bundles the copied attributes so callers can use the freshly created object immediately for drawing or further manipulation.

@lcmNewLineStyle::cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14c.body: Creates a new line‑style object, initializing its member data with default settings (no‑op‑or‑no‑arguments).

@lcmNewLineStyle::~cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNewLineStyle::~cmNewLineStyle@k_ZN14.body: Creates a new line‑style instance, wiring its internal parameters and returning a reference that callers can use to adjust the line’s visual attributes.

@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.body: Creates an object by taking a string argument and forwarding it (by moving) to initialize its base‑class member. The constructor itself does nothing else.

@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.body: The `cmNinjaBuild` public constructor initializes a build‑plan object that parses a Ninja build file, extracts the relevant build‑type information from the parsed AST, and registers the corresponding “cmNinja” generator with the parser. It accepts only the parsed build‑file, performs validation, and stores the resulting configuration for later code‑generation steps.

@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.body:
Creates a new build instance that mirrors every configuration and state of the supplied object.  
During construction it validates the incoming data, guarantees no shared mutable resources, and properly re‑initialises any owned handles or caches so the new instance can operate independently.  
It also guards against accidental self‑assignment and shallow copy pitfalls that could leave dangling references or duplicated ownership semantics.

@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaBuild::cmNinjaBuild@k_ZN12cmNin.body: cmNinjaBuild is called during project setup to initialize the build system with the default configuration. It runs once per build session, resetting the internal state of the Ninja build engine so that subsequent build steps start from a clean baseline.

@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::Convert.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::Convert.body: The function hands the supplied library string to the internal `GG` component’s `ConvertToNinjaPath` method and returns the resulting path string.

@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::cmNinja.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::cmNinja.body: This constructor simply forwards the supplied `outputConverter` and `stateDir` to the base class (`cmLinkLineDeviceComputer`) and stores the pointer to the global generator (`gg`) in the member `GG`. No additional logic is performed in the body.

@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::cmNinja.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::cmNinja.body: This constructor is deleted, so objects of the type cannot be copied, preventing inadvertent duplication of internal state.

@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::operato.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::operato.body: The assignment operator copies the internal state from the RHS instance into the current object, then returns a reference to the assigned instance so that further calls can be chained.

@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::~cmNinj.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer::~cmNinj.body: The destructor `~cmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer()` is invoked when an object of `cmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer` is destroyed. It performs the necessary cleanup for this concrete implementation – releasing any resources (e.g., sockets, file handles, allocated buffers) that were acquired during its lifetime, ensuring that any underlying `cmLinkLineDeviceComputer` resources are properly released, and then delegating to the base class destructor to finalize the teardown.

@lcmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator::CheckUse.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator::CheckUse.body: This helper inspects the build‑time environment for a flag named `CMAKE_<LIB>_USE_RESPONSE_FILE_FOR_LIBRARIES`. It looks up that variable; if the variable exists, the function returns whether its value is “on” (truthy), otherwise it simply falls back to the default, which is `true`. The method is `const` so it guarantees no modification of internal state while performing the check.

@lcmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator::ComputeD.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator::ComputeD.body: The function `ComputeDeviceLinkCmd` builds and returns a vector of command strings used for CUDA device linking.
